passage: I'm Shalini, and I shared a flat in Frankfurt with Rehana last winter. The first time our German neighbour, Frau Keller, offered her cake, Rehana smiled and said, 'No, no, thank you,' the way we do at home, waiting for the second offer. It never came. Frau Keller simply nodded and put the cake away. Rehana's face fell a little. Later, when Rehana invited Frau Keller for biryani, she insisted three times; Frau Keller looked uneasy and took a tiny spoonful. The next time, I watched Rehana say, 'Yes, please, just a small piece,' and Frau Keller beamed. I think they both learnt something, though neither said so.

qa.q: What did Frau Keller offer Rehana the first time?
qa.a: Cake.

qa.q: What does Shalini's last line suggest Shalini felt watching the two neighbours?
qa.a: Shalini felt amused and fond, watching both of them slowly and quietly learn each other's rules.

qa.q: What could Rehana and Frau Keller each do to avoid such awkward moments?
qa.a: Learn the local rule: Rehana can accept directly, and Frau Keller can know that an Indian host may insist out of warmth, not pressure.

qa.q: How did Rehana seem to feel when the second offer never came?
qa.a: Rehana seemed disappointed and a little embarrassed, since at home a first 'no' is only politeness.

grounding: Shows a young person observing that one culture expects the host to insist and the guest to refuse, while another takes a first no as final, and how learning the local rule eases awkwardness.

passage:
Monday: At her colleague Raghav's home in Delhi, Lalremsiami, twenty-four, politely declines a third helping of rajma. Raghav's mother puts two more spoonfuls on her plate anyway. In Lalremsiami's family in Aizawl, a clear no is taken as final, so she eats slowly and says nothing.
Wednesday: Over office tea she asks Raghav about it. He laughs. 'In our house the first no means maybe, and the second means please insist. Mummy thought you were being shy.'
Saturday: At the next visit, when Raghav's mother offers more, Lalremsiami smiles and says, 'Aunty, I'm truly full. Your rajma is too good.' His mother laughs and, for once, puts the ladle down.

qa.q: What dish was Lalremsiami offered more of?
qa.a: Rajma.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she ate the extra spoonfuls slowly?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and confused, too polite to protest but unsure why her clear no had been ignored.

qa.q: What helped Lalremsiami handle the next offer?
qa.a: Asking Raghav about the custom, then declining warmly and praising the food, so Aunty could hear the no as real.

qa.q: How had Raghav's mother seen Lalremsiami's refusals?
qa.a: She thought Lalremsiami was being shy, since in her house a guest's first refusals invite the host to insist.

grounding: Illustrates a young person noticing that one family expects the host to insist past a guest's refusals while her own takes a first no as final, and learning the local rule to avoid awkwardness.

passage:
Varun, you leave for Amsterdam next week, so let your Parveen Khala tell you about my first English tea.

I was twenty-four, a new nurse in Leeds, invited to my ward sister's house. She asked, "Would you like a cup of tea?" And I said, "No, no, please don't trouble," the way we do in Lucknow, waiting for her to insist twice.

She said, "Right-o," and poured one for herself.

I sat there for an hour, dying of thirst, too proud to ask. On the bus home I laughed until I cried.

The next week a friend from Glasgow explained: here, a no is a no. So at the next visit, when she asked, I said, "Yes, please, milk and one sugar." She smiled as if I'd given her a present.

And when she came to my flat, I insisted three times, and she looked terrified!

qa.q: Where was Parveen working at twenty-four?
qa.a: Parveen was a new nurse in Leeds.

qa.q: What did young Parveen feel sitting without tea for an hour?
qa.a: Parveen felt thirsty and embarrassed, too proud to ask after refusing the way she would in Lucknow.

qa.q: What turning point helped Parveen with English hospitality?
qa.a: A friend from Glasgow explaining that a no there is final, so the next time she simply said yes.

qa.q: How might the ward sister have felt when Parveen insisted three times at her flat?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and a bit alarmed, since where she came from one offer is enough.

grounding: Shows a young person discovering that one culture expects refusing and insisting while another takes a first no as final.

passage:
Damini had forty minutes to catch the last bus back to her flat in Amman, and Zainab's mother was not letting her leave.

"One more piece of knafeh!"

"No, thank you, I'm full."

The plate came anyway. Damini ate it. Then came the coffee. She drank one tiny cup; it was refilled at once. A second; refilled again. She glanced at the clock, panicking.

Zainab leaned over, laughing. "Shake the cup side to side when you're done. Otherwise my mother thinks you're just being polite."

Damini tilted the cup gently from side to side. Zainab's mother smiled, took it, and finally let her stand.

On the bus, Damini laughed to herself. At home in Nagpur she did exactly this to guests, insisting till they gave in. She had never once wondered how it felt from the other side.

qa.q: How long did Damini have to catch the last bus?
qa.a: Damini had forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as her coffee cup kept being refilled?
qa.a: Damini felt panicked and a little embarrassed, full, watching the clock, and unsure how to refuse politely.

qa.q: What local rule helped Damini, and why?
qa.a: Shaking the cup side to side signals you're finished; knowing it let her decline without offending her host.

qa.q: How might Zainab's mother see Damini's first 'No, thank you'?
qa.a: She took it as polite modesty, not a real no, so she kept offering the way her custom expects.

grounding: Shows a young person abroad discovering a host who insists past a first refusal, and learning the local signal that avoids both offence and awkwardness.

passage:
Sumit had warned his mother that Ritu grew up in Hamburg, but Mummy still did what she always did.

"Take more rajma, beta."

"No, thank you, I'm fine," Ritu said.

Mummy heaped two more spoons on anyway. Ritu's smile froze, and she ate every grain.

Later it went the other way. Sumit's little cousin said no to Ritu's homemade biscuits, expecting her to insist. Ritu simply nodded and closed the tin. His cousin stared at it, crushed.

In the car Sumit laughed. "In my house the first no means nothing. The third no means maybe."

"In mine, no means no," Ritu said. "I was so full I couldn't breathe."

"Next time say, 'I'm really full, Aunty, it was lovely.' And my cousin will learn to say yes the first time."

qa.q: Where did Ritu grow up?
qa.a: Ritu grew up in Hamburg.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling as he watched the two mix-ups?
qa.a: Sumit was amused and sympathetic, laughing in the car as both his mother's and Ritu's rules misfired.

qa.q: What does Sumit suggest for next time?
qa.a: Ritu can say 'I'm really full, Aunty, it was lovely' so the no sounds final, and his cousin can learn to say yes the first time.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Mummy heaped on more rajma?
qa.a: Ritu felt awkward and overfull; her smile froze, but she ate it all to be polite.

grounding: Shows a young person noticing that his family insists past a first no while a friend takes a first no as final, and how knowing the rule avoids awkwardness.

passage:
"Noor, did I do something wrong? Pieter left hungry."
"What happened, Eshaan?"
"I asked if he wanted more biryani. He said, 'No, thank you.' So I said, 'Arre, have a little.' He said no again. Then I put some on his plate anyway, like my mother does."
"And?"
"He looked really uncomfortable. He didn't eat it."
Noor laughed softly. "In your mother's house, a guest says no twice to be polite, and the host insists. Here in Amsterdam, no means no."
"So I was forcing food on him?"
"A bit, yes. And your aunt last month in Lucknow, remember? I said 'no, thank you' once and she never offered again. I went to bed hungry."
Eshaan groaned. "So it's the opposite for each of us."
"Exactly. Ask once here. Ask three times in Lucknow."
"I'll message Pieter tomorrow. And save him some biryani."

qa.q: What did Eshaan do after Pieter said no twice?
qa.a: Eshaan put some on Pieter's plate anyway, like Eshaan's mother does.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when the polite no in Lucknow was taken as final?
qa.a: Noor probably felt embarrassed and a bit awkward, too polite to ask again and going to bed hungry.

qa.q: What rule does Noor suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Ask once in Amsterdam and three times in Lucknow; knowing the local rule avoids both offence and awkwardness.

qa.q: How did Pieter probably experience the extra biryani?
qa.a: Pieter probably felt uncomfortable and pressured, since for him a first no was final, so he left it uneaten.

grounding: It illustrates a young person noticing that some cultures expect insisting and refusing twice while others take a first no as final.
